intro: You'll learn Latin American Spanish first, but you live near Madrid – so here's everything that differs, side by side. Everyone understands both versions!

grammar.title: “You all”: ustedes vs vosotros
grammar.note: Vosotros has its own verb forms (-áis, -éis, -ís) and pronoun os: ¿Os gusta? Only Spain uses it. Conjugation tables in this app mark it with 🇪🇸 only.

grammar.title: Talking about today: pretérito vs pretérito perfecto
grammar.note: For yesterday and earlier, both use the pretérito: Ayer comí paella.

grammar.title: Tú and usted
grammar.note: Spain uses tú with almost everyone. Mexico, Colombia and much of Latin America use usted more with strangers and older people. In Argentina and Uruguay you'll also hear vos instead of tú.

grammar.title: Watch out: coger
grammar.note: Coger is a totally normal verb in Spain (to take, to catch), but in Mexico and much of Latin America it's vulgar slang. Use tomar there.

pronunciation.title: Seseo 🌎 vs distinción 🇪🇸
pronunciation.explanation: Latin America pronounces c (before e/i) and z like “s”. Central and northern Spain pronounce them like the English “th” in “think”. Listen to both voices:

pronunciation.title: The j and g sound
pronunciation.explanation: J (and g before e/i) is a breathy “h” in most of Latin America, and a stronger, raspy sound from the throat in Spain – like the “ch” in Scottish “loch”.

usage.title: Greetings
usage.text:
Spain: two kisses on the cheek (right cheek first) between women and between men and women, even when meeting for the first time.
Latin America: usually one kiss on the right cheek, or a handshake in formal settings.

usage.title: Meal times
usage.text:
Spain: lunch (la comida) at 2–3 pm, dinner (la cena) at 9–10 pm.
Mexico: la comida is also the big meal, around 2–4 pm; dinner is lighter.

usage.title: Filler words you'll hear
usage.text:
🇪🇸 vale, tío/tía, guay, pues, venga (come on / OK, bye)
🌎 órale (MX), chévere (CO/VE), bacán (CL/PE), ¿mande? (MX, polite “pardon?”)
